newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Second EMU wave expected after two years.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Second EMU wave expected after two years.

text.p: Spain, Portugal and Italy are expected to join Europes single currency club two years after its launch, according to a Reuters survey.
The poll of 45 economists across Europe showed that the likelihood of the three countries joining in the first wave on January 1, 1999, were low and sinking further.

The survey, conducted on March 10 and 11, showed an average likelihood of only 24 percent that Portugal would enter EMU in the first wave, while Spain's chances were seen at 18 percent and Italy just seven percent.
This compares with 29, 31 and seven percent respectively in the February survey.
Those analysts who doubted the first-wave membership of Spain, Portugal and Italy, often dubbed the Club Med countries, gave an average prediction of a two-year delay before entry.
Analysts say there was a need to make a separate judgment on their entry prospects, rather than treating the three countries in a single category.
"We dont buy this Club Med name because there is no club at all," said Serge Le Gal, French economist at Caisse des Depots in Paris.
You could argue that if the UK doesnt go ahead then Ireland wont either. The same goes for Portugal joining without Spain.
Peter van den Houte, senior economist at Bank Brussels Lambert, said there was a strong tendency to group the Iberian nations.
A Spain-Portugal link is much stronger than a Spain-Italy one. Spain will come very close to the criteria but theoretically, it could be possible that Portugal joins and Spain doesnt, he said.
The average delay before all 15 European Union nations joined EMU ranged from one to four years, according to the survey.
Austria was forecast by all but one of the economists as a first-wave starter. The one prediction for a delay put Austria's entry after two years.

The likelihood of Ireland and Finland joining from the start was put on average at 84 and 82 percent respectively, and those predicting a delay said they expected Ireland to join a year after the launch and Finland 18 months later.

Sweden and Denmark, each struggling with political and constitutional obstacles to EMU, were rated in the survey with only an 11 and 13 percent likelihood of joining from the start, and the survey gave an average prediction that Sweden would enter the single currency club two years after launch, and Denmark a year after that.
Britain and Greece, both rated as no-hopers for EMUs first wave, were expected on average to join the club three years and four years later.
At least one of the forecasters was even more pessimistic about EMU going ahead altogether, Not in my lifetime! said Dan McLaughlin at Riada Stockbrokers in Dublin.
